sources.news_title: Blanche says ‘one-sided news’ is a national security issue worthy of barring press
sources.text:
Blanche says ‘one-sided news’ is a national security issue worthy of barring press
By Aileen Graef, CNN
(CNN) — Attorney General Todd Blanche said on Sunday that media outlets reporting what the Trump administration considers to be “one-sided” news is a national security issue severe enough to justify banning the press from gaining access to the White House and Air Force One.
“By the way, that is what is a national security problem. When you have completely misinformation, complete misinformation coming out of the White House, that affects our relationship with our foreign partners. That affects our relationship with our foreign enemies,” Blanche said in an interview on ABC’s This Week.
The attorney general’s definition of what constitutes a national security risk elaborates on a government claim made in a court filing seeking to justify President Donald Trump’s effort to implement such a ban against CNN, MSNOW and Politico, which a federal judge overseeing that case has greeted with skepticism.
Judge Timothy Kelly ordered the Trump administration to temporarily restore the credentials of CNN, MSNOW, and Politico journalists affected by the ban, saying the revocation was done without “constitutionally adequate due process.” He also pushed back on the argument from the Justice Department that it was on the basis of national security, saying the articles cited by the government were “routine” and that the government’s arguments “offer little to back up their asserted national security interest.”
“For one thing, nothing in the record that predates this suit suggests that the revocation of Plaintiffs’ hard passes was motivated by national security concerns,” Kelly wrote. “Certainly, that is not what President Trump said when he announced that he was ‘banning’ Plaintiffs from the White House — instead, he focused on the alleged lack of truthfulness and negativity of Plaintiffs’ reporting.”
The government cited reports from the outlets that referred to information provided by “senior White House officials” as a national security concern. Blanche said the administration’s concern was rather that the reporting was “one-sided.”
“What I’m talking about is the government’s position and what the Department of Justice said in court, which is the same thing that President Trump has said repeatedly, which is at some point, at some point, the complete misinformation and the inaccuracy and the one-sided news out of certain organizations does become a national security issue, and it’s not right for the people of the United States to have to put up with it,” Blanche said. He did not offer any details to support his claims of inaccuracy.
In an exchange last week with US Ambassador to the United Nations Mike Waltz, CNN’s Kaitlan Collins noted that one CNN report he cited about concerns over a shortage of munitions during the Iran War, was based on a Pentagon Inspector General’s report.
Despite being let back into the White House complex, the White House barred CNN from flying on Air Force One on Saturday as part of the news outlet’s duties covering the president on behalf of major television networks.
CNN had been scheduled to fly aboard the president’s plane on his trip to Tennessee for a college football game as part of the White House TV press pool — a small, rotating group of journalists that cover the president in areas where space is limited and share the information they gather with other TV networks. On Sunday, Fox News was allowed to handle its regularly scheduled pool duties for the president’s trip to Chicago, where he attended the Presidents Cup golf tournament.
In an appearance on CNN’s “State of the Union” Sunday, Waltz echoed Blanche, saying “media bias across the board” is something that “needs to be fixed.”
“There is a negative agenda. There is a negative narrative, and then we’re going to get anonymous sources. Heck, I just saw a story where anonymous sources were referring to a now dead senator. So, yeah, this needs to be fixed. And President Trump is quite frustrated with this, this media bias across the board,” he said.

sources.news_title: Justice Department chief backs up Trump's right to ban CNN reporters from Air Force One
Todd Blanche says media coverage can become national security issue
sources.text:
Attorney General Todd Blanche on Sunday defended the Trump administration's restrictions on several news organizations, arguing that certain media coverage can become a national security issue as the White House remains embroiled in a legal battle over press access.
Speaking on ABC News' This Week, Blanche backed President Donald Trump's decision to bar CNN from traveling aboard Air Force One for a trip to Tennessee on Saturday and reiterated the administration's position that access to the White House is not guaranteed.
"It is a privilege to be in the White House for anybody," Blanche told moderator Martha Raddatz. Later in the interview, he added: "It is the people's house. It is a privilege, not a right, to be there."
The comments come days after U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly temporarily blocked the administration from enforcing its ban on CNN, Politico and MS NOW while their lawsuit proceeds. The three outlets argue the restrictions violate the First Amendment and amount to retaliation for unfavorable coverage.
Following the ban, the White House launched its own streaming channel, Trump TV.
Newsweek reached out to the White House and the Justice Department for comments on Sunday.
Blanche Defends White House Restrictions
Raddatz pressed Blanche repeatedly on the administration's decision to exclude CNN, which had been scheduled to serve as the rotating television pool network during Trump's Tennessee trip.
"The president has every right to decide who gets to fly on his plane," Blanche said, referring to Air Force One.
Blanche argued that inaccurate reporting can harm U.S. interests abroad.
"What we expect and it is for the protection of our country, so that when foreign leaders, when foreign governments, when citizens that are around the world hear what's happening in the administration, that it happens to be accurate," he said.
The attorney general also claimed that "the complete misinformation and the inaccuracy and the one-sided news out of certain organizations does become a national security issue."
Those comments touched on an issue central to the administration's ongoing court fight over the restrictions.
In his order, Kelly, who was appointed by Trump during his first term, wrote that "nothing in the record that predates this suit suggests that the revocation of Plaintiffs' hard passes was motivated by national security concerns" and noted that Trump had instead focused on the outlets' allegedly negative and inaccurate coverage when announcing the restrictions. He also said the court was "skeptical" that safeguarding national security was the administration's actual motivation for revoking the credentials.
Kelly further wrote that the administration had offered little evidence that revoking the outlets' credentials would protect national security, saying the record lacked factual support for that claim.
Raddatz challenged that assertion on Sunday, pointing out that Trump initially justified the restrictions by accusing outlets of unfair coverage rather than citing security concerns.
"The president said nothing about national security when he announced this ban," she said.
"Well, I'm not going to get into what the judge says," Blanche responded. "That litigation is ongoing, but our position has been clear from the beginning. What they say is exactly the issue when it comes to national security."
The dispute stems from Trump's decision earlier this month to ban CNN, Politico and MS NOW from the White House, saying the outlets had repeatedly published inaccurate coverage.
The president has defended the move on Truth Social, writing that media organizations "shouldn't be able to constantly write or report FICTION and LIES" while covering the administration.
After the outlets sued the White House, Kelly issued a temporary restraining order restoring their press credentials for 14 days while litigation continues.
Trump and White House Defend Ban
The president has argued that the dispute is not about suppressing journalism but about limiting access for organizations he says spread false information.
Following the lawsuit from the banned outlets, Trump wrote that the White House was not attacking a free press but rather fighting what he described as "FAKE NEWS." He later argued that outlets that publish what he describes as false reporting should not receive special access to the president.
"It is a threat to our National Security, and must be stopped, NOW!" he wrote on Truth Social.
Vice President JD Vance said the affected organizations are not being prevented from reporting but are being denied what he described as special access.
"He's not banning media outlets," Vance said earlier this week. "We're not going to give you special access to the White House if you engage in what is effectively propaganda."
The Trump administration has consistently argued that the dispute concerns access, not censorship. In court filings, the Justice Department contended that White House credentials are "a privilege, not a right" and that the First Amendment protects an outlet's ability to publish without guaranteeing a hard pass, briefing-room seat or place in the press pool.
The president has also maintained that the restrictions are about a broader pattern of coverage rather than any single article. Asked about the decision earlier this month, Trump told reporters there was "no particular reason" and described it as the result of "cumulative stories over the last two years."
The dispute has also disrupted the traditional television press pool, with ABC, CBS, NBC and Fox News refusing to replace CNN when it was removed from scheduled pool assignments.
What Happens Next
The judge set a schedule for both parties to argue if the court should issue a longer preliminary injunction, with CNN, MS NOW and Politico having until Monday to file their motion while the White House is given until Friday, October 2 to respond. After that, the outlets may reply by Monday, October 5.
Kelly said he "intends to rule expeditiously" on the preliminary injunction request. The current court order restoring the outlets’ access ends on Thursday, October 8.
Newsweek’s reporters and editors used Martyn, our AI assistant, to produce this story. Learn more about Martyn here.
Contact Newsweek editors for this story: Steve Mollman and Anthony Murray.

sources.news_title: Blanche claims Trump ‘hasn’t denied access’ to White House reporters

sources.text:
Attorney General Todd Blanche on Sunday addressed the Trump administration's decision to ban three mainstream news outlets from accessing the White House, saying that President Donald Trump had not "denied access" to the organizations and asserting that it is a "privilege ... not a right" to be at the White House.
"The president hasn't denied access. That's not the right way to describe it. This is -- what the president has said is that he is sick and tired of certain media outlets just refusing to report accurate news," Blanche said in an exclusive interview with "This Week" co-anchor Martha Raddatz. "There's still obviously litigation going on, but the important thing, Martha, is to know that ... being in the White House is a privilege. It's not a right."
In the early hours Thursday, Judge Timothy Kelly issued a temporary restraining order that required the White House to temporarily restore credentials of journalists working for CNN, MS NOW and Politico. Kelly said in his ruling that he believed the outlets cleared the "high bar" required to grant a TRO.
Journalists were allowed back onto the White House grounds later Thursday and primary television pool coverage resumed Friday for the final day of Chinese President Xi Jinping's official state visit. But on Saturday, there was no TV pool coverage for the president's trip to a football game in Tennessee; CNN was scheduled to be network covering the president that day, but they said their access to Air Force One was blocked.
Blanche said it wasn't unusual for a news outlet to not be allowed onto the president's plane.
"The White House routinely decides who can go on Air Force One. This wasn't a a one-time denial of CNN. There's all kinds of times when certain reporters are not flying or are flying," according to Blanche, who added, "it's not unusual, and as a matter of fact, it's common every time the president travels that he and his team decide which reporters get to travel with the president."
Blanche claimed the three news outlets that were subject to the White House ban "refuse to report anything accurately," which he said presented a "national security problem."
"When you have complete misinformation coming out of the White House that affects our relationship with our foreign partners, that affects our relationship with our foreign enemies -- and so this is just not about the fact that they're refusing to report accurate news. It's all about the information that the American people have a right to hear coming out of of our what should be respected media outlets."
Judge Kelly, however, was skeptical in his TRO ruling that national security was the true reason for the ban.
"For one thing, nothing in the record that predates this suit suggests that the revocation of Plaintiffs’ hard passes was motivated by national security concerns. Certainly, that is not what President Trump said when he announced that he was 'banning' Plaintiffs from the White House -- instead, he focused on the alleged lack of truthfulness and negativity of Plaintiffs’ reporting," Kelly wrote.
Hours after announcing the ban on social media, Trump was asked in the Oval Office if there was any "particular reason or particular story" that prompted it.
"No, no. It's -- it's really just cumulative stories over the last two years. You get sick of it," the president said.
On "This Week," Blanche said he wouldn't "get into what the judge says" because the litigation is ongoing, but added "our position has been clear from the beginning. What they say is exactly the issue when it comes to national security."
When Raddatz pressed Blanche to provide specific examples of stories with which the White House has taken issue, Blanche declined to do so.
Artificial intelligence 'vital to our national security'
On the issue of artificial intelligence, the attorney general echoed the president's position on the technology, describing it as "so important and vital to our national security interests and to the success of this country that the United States lead in this space."
Trump has said it's critical that the U.S. continues to dominate the AI space, citing competition with China specifically.
"Whoever wins AI, WINS! We are leading now over China, and everyone else, and I’m going to keep it that way! I’m not going to stifle Growth, of something that will be bigger than the Industrial Revolution, or the Internet, itself," he posted on social media Monday.
Some AI company leaders are calling for an industry-wide slowdown amid growing concerns about how the rapid pace of development. Multiple incidents of AI agents acting autonomously have come to light in recent months, including instances where AI agents infiltrated outside companies without the agents' parent companies' awareness as it happened.
Last week, Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said that OpenAI agent "infiltrated" a government public health website earlier this summer. This weekend, OpenAI confirmed that its models interacted with U.S. government websites in unexpected ways, behavior the company discovered amid an ongoing review into its AI agents' behaviors.
Blanche acknowledged that "there's going to be adjustments that have to be made" around AI as the industry continues to develop, but he argued the companies themselves already have the ability to "adjust the technology" as needed.
"In the meantime, the answer is not to just try to all of a sudden try to regulate this in a way that will make us second or third place in the world as far as being being the leaders in this space," Blanche said.
During his speech at the United Nations General Assembly in New York Tuesday, Trump said of AI, "We're going to watch it closely through the Department of Justice."
Asked what that meant, Blanche said, "What it means is that we have a ton of laws -- criminal laws, civil laws -- that are already in place and on the books that allow us to charge individuals, to charge companies in the right circumstances when there's crimes committed, and so the answer isn't always more laws, more laws, more laws."
"When there are crimes committed, we have a lot of tools already, and the federal Title 18 gives us a lot of a lot of ways to go after criminals and bad actors in the AI space and other spaces," Blanche continued. "So when the president talks about about the fact that the Department of Justice and the FBI and [Homeland Security Investigations], they can go and arrest bad actors in this space, that's what he means, and it's true, and that's what we're doing."

sources.news_title: Todd Blanche snaps when pressed on Trump's 'unconstitutional' move: 'I did not say that!'
sources.text:
Attorney General Todd Blanche snapped at ABC News’ Martha Raddatz Sunday after being pressed on President Donald Trump’s latest attack on the media that has been described as “flatly unconstitutional."
Trump banned three major outlets from the White House earlier this month after accusing them of reporting “fake news,” a decision that legal experts argued to be a blatant violation of the First Amendment. Last week, a federal judge temporarily blocked Trump’s media ban, only for the Trump administration to continue barring the outlets from the White House.
The Justice Department has argued that the three media outlets’ reporting has jeopardized national security, and on Sunday, Blanche was asked to provide specifics.
“What [the media outlets] say is exactly the issue when it comes to national security,” Blanche told Raddatz.
Raddatz then bluntly asked Blanche to provide an example of how the media outlets’ reporting had jeopardized or threatened national security — a question Blanche sidestepped by interpreting it to be referencing general inaccurate reporting.
“I’m sorry, give you an example of when CNN doesn’t report accurately? You cannot be asking me that!” Blanche said.
“At some point, the complete misinformation and the inaccuracy and the one-sided news out of certain organizations does become a national security issue, and it’s not right for the people of the United States to have to put up with it!”
In an apparent attempt to gain insight on how the Trump administration may address the supposed national security threats from media outlets’ reporting, Raddatz asked how the matter might be handled.
“So are you saying you’re going to screen people before they get on a flight coming to the White House?” Raddatz asked.
Blanche was not pleased with Raddatz’s question.
“I did not say that!” Blanche snapped. “You don’t get to put words in my mouth, that’s not the way it works! I didn’t say that. You said I said something that I didn’t say!”
Wow -- a haggard-sounded Blanche crashes and burns on ABC while trying to defend Trump's ban on the free press
RADDATZ: The president said nothing about national security when he announced this ban, and clearly you're very interested in what the press says and how they say it… pic.twitter.com/kaXC8nw7z2
— Aaron Rupar (@atrupar) September 27, 2026

sources.news_title: AG Blanche addresses White House news outlet ban amid litigation, calls access 'a privilege ... not a right'
AG Todd Blanche Addresses Media Coverage Concerns
sources.text:
In a recent statement, Attorney General Todd Blanche underscored President Trump's growing frustration with certain media outlets, accusing them of failing to deliver accurate news to the public. AG Blanche emphasized that the privilege of accessing the White House has been taken for granted by some members of the press.
White House Access Called a Privilege
AG Blanche conveyed the President's sentiment that being in the White House is a privilege and not an inherent right. He stated, "President Trump is sick and tired of certain media outlets just refusing to report accurate news." This stems from what the administration views as continuous one-sided coverage that does not serve the interests of the American populace.
President Trump's Public Visibility
Despite allegations of denied access, AG Blanche clarified that this characterization is incorrect. "The president hasn't denied access. That's not the right way to describe it," he stated. He noted that President Trump was visible to many Americans, referencing his recent public appearance at a football game in Tennessee. The President was not hidden from the public eye, contrary to what some reports might suggest.
Continued Legal and Media Disputes
While acknowledging ongoing litigation, AG Blanche highlighted the unmatched opportunities that members of the press have when covering the White House. He remarked, "It is a privilege to be in the White House for anybody." The ongoing dispute underscores a larger debate about the relationship between the media and the current administration, with the President advocating for a fairer portrayal within media narratives.
The administration's assertion calls for introspection among media outlets about their role and responsibilities in covering the presidency. The upcoming developments in this legal tussle will likely set precedents for press engagement with the White House.

Blanche says Trump ‘hasn’t denied access’ after reporters barred from White House grounds
Attorney General Todd Blanche said Sept. 27, 2026, that President Trump has not denied access to White House reporters after the administration barred reporters from CNN, Politico and MS NOW from the White House grounds and the Secret Service confiscated their passes, The Hill reported.
Blanche made the remark on ABC’s This Week to host Martha Raddatz, saying, “Well, the president hasn’t denied access,” The Hill reported.
The Hill published the report on Sept. 27, 2026.
